#6634. Chocolate-Covered Strawberry Turkeys

Turkey is the star of Thanksgiving dinner, but it can also be the star of dessert if you stretch your imagination enough. This idea first gained popularity on TikTok, using chocolate-dipped strawberries, marshmallows, pretzel rods, and melted chocolate to create these adorable little treats.

They're so simple to make: To make a leg, you spear two mini marshmallows with half a pretzel rod, then use kitchen shears to trim the edges into a long oval shape. Repeat for a second leg, then cut one mini marshmallow diagonally in half to make the wings. You'll stick these to the strawberry with a dab of melted chocolate (which acts as your glue), then let that sit to adhere. All that's left is a quick bath in melted chocolate.

#6633. Homemade Dog Treats With Applesauce and Cheese

These homemade dog treats are crunchy, cheesy, and enthusiastically approved by my little curmudgeon. The recipe began with a dog biscuit from the December 2005 issue of Gourmet. While the generous quantities of butter, brown sugar, and salt in the original gave me pause, I used it as inspiration for these cracker-like treats, swapping in ingredients I’d discussed with my vet and knew my pup would love. I’m hoping yours will too.

Whole wheat flour provides structure plus fiber, while brown rice flour helps the biscuits bake up crisp. Old-fashioned rolled oats give the treats a pleasantly nubby texture. The dough comes together with an egg and unsweetened applesauce. Be sure to check the applesauce label for added sweeteners, especially xylitol, which is toxic to dogs.

I like Gouda for its aroma—it drives my dog into a frenzy—but sharp cheddar or Swiss will work too. Curly parsley and mint lend a fresh herbal note and mild breath freshening, but the real secret ingredient is a little anise seed. Sometimes called “dog nip,” anise has a scent that some dogs find irresistible. Fennel seed makes a fine substitute.

Can I make these homemade dog treats with pumpkin?

Absolutely. For a fall-inspired variation, use plain canned pumpkin purée instead of applesauce, oat flour instead of brown rice flour, sage instead of parsley, and sharp cheddar for the cheese. (Honestly, add a little salt and you could serve these on a Thanksgiving charcuterie board.) For your dog, though, skip the salt and be sure to use 100% pumpkin purée, not pumpkin pie filling, which contains added sugar and spices.

IF USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Pulse 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a food processor to combine (about three 1-second pulses). Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar, ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed, and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed, and pulse to incorporate (two to three 1-second pulses). Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg, and pulse until a coarse dough forms, about 20 seconds. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

IF NOT USING A FOOD PROCESSOR: Whisk 1 cup (113 g) whole wheat flour, ¾ cup (96 g) brown rice flour, ¾ cup (76 g) old-fashioned rolled oats, 1 tsp. baking powder, ½ tsp. ground fennel seed, and ½ tsp. ground ginger in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup (4 oz.) shredded Gouda or sharp cheddar and toss to coat the cheese. Finely chop ¼ cup curly parsley leaves and tender stems, packed and ¼ cup mint leaves, packed; set aside. Create a well in center of flour mixture. Add ¾ cup unsweetened applesauce and 1 large egg to well and mix with a wooden spoon, bringing flour into center until combined. Fold in chopped herbs. (You can roll out dough right away, but it’s much easier to work with it if you let it chill first.) Divide dough into two rounds and wrap each in plastic, or place in separate resealable containers, and refrigerate for at least 30 minutes and up to 24 hours.

Bake dog treats, rotating baking sheets front to back and top to bottom halfway through, until cheese has bubbled up and treats have darkened slightly, 12–15 minutes.

Do Ahead: Dog treats can be baked, cooled, and stored at room temperature in an airtight container for up to 3 weeks or frozen for 3 months.

A mysterious bronze foot found in a bog was likely once part of a monumental statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius, who tried to conquer Scotland.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

All that remains of a larger-than-life statue of the Roman emperor Antoninus Pius once erected in Scotland is a lower right leg. Experts have now reconstructed what the entire sculpture looked like but are still unsure why it was carefully dismantled over 1,800 years ago.

The gold-covered bronze foot and calf, also known as the Milsington leg, was discovered in a bog in 1820, according to a Nov. 12 statement from National Museums Scotland. It is the only example of a monumental Roman emperor statue ever found in Scotland and was likely made around A.D. 140.

Initially, experts thought the bronze statue had been looted from York, England, which was founded by the Romans in A.D. 71 as the town of Eboracum. But as research into the Roman frontier advanced over the years, it became clear that equestrian statues were often set up in forts along the border of the Roman Empire.

This lower leg, experts now believe, originally came from an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius that was similar to the famous statue of Marcus Aurelius in Rome.

Antoninus Pius was Roman emperor from A.D. 138 to 161, succeeding Hadrian, who had built an enormous wall to defend the northernmost limit of the Roman Empire. To add to Rome's territory, Antoninus Pius directed the imperial governor of Roman Britain to move north, invade southern Scotland and build a second wall, called the Antonine Wall. But that wall was left undefended after Antoninus Pius died, and the Romans retreated from Scotland.

During that retreat, the Romans may have dismantled any valuable statues that they had set up, according to the statement. An examination of the Milsington leg ahead of a new exhibition showed that the bronze had no cut marks, suggesting it was removed carefully and not "brutally hacked off."

"This contrasts with examples of statues being deliberately destroyed after a battle, when an emperor's memory was condemned, or when they were chopped up for scrap," according to National Museums Scotland.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

With the Scottish provenance firmly established, National Museums Scotland curators were able to learn more about Antoninus Pius and his approach to imperial expansion.

"This really turns on its head our understanding of Rome's second attempt at conquering Scotland," Fraser Hunter, principal curator of prehistoric art and Roman archaeology at National Museums Scotland, said in the statement. "This was a big deal for the Emperor, something which was worth celebrating."

But while the boot-clad bronze leg provides a glimpse into the monuments that may have graced southern Scotland nearly two millennia ago, it raises an important question for Hunter: Where is the rest of the statue?

The Milsington leg, the Inveresk Mithras altars and other Roman-period finds are on display beginning Nov. 14 in the exhibit "Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire" at the National Museum of Scotland.

#6631. Is Pink Turkey Safe to Eat?

Pink turkey doesn't necessarily mean your Thanksgiving feast is ruined. Here's how to know if your bird is safe to eat so you can stay calm and turkey on.

I’ll never forget the Thanksgiving when I was convinced I’d ruined the holiday for everyone. I wasn’t an experienced cook at the time, and it was one of my first attempts at making a Thanksgiving turkey. I used a helpful guide for how long to cook a turkey and even invested in a meat thermometer to be sure it reached at least 165°F. It looked great, and I was so proud!

Imagine my surprise and horror when I carved that gorgeously browned roast turkey and discovered it was pink inside. I was so nervous my guests would assume the turkey was undercooked. I didn’t know then that pink turkey can be perfectly safe to eat—as long as it’s cooked to that vital internal temperature.

Cooked turkey can look pink for a few reasons that have nothing to do with doneness, including the age of the bird, how it’s prepared and natural pigmentation.

“Poultry naturally can have a pink hue,” says Heidi Diestel of turkey farm Diestel Family Ranch in Sonora, California. “The legs and thighs have more of the natural pigments that give meat its darker color. Those pigments, along with changes that happen during cooking, can leave some pink even when the turkey is fully cooked.”

The pigments Heidi refers to are proteins called myoglobin and cytochrome c. The more of these proteins the meat has, the darker it will be. Older animals tend to have more proteins, and therefore darker pigmentation, as do any regularly exercised muscles. That explains why leg meat is darker than breast meat, as turkeys spend the bulk of their days walking and running.

Cooking can also cause a chemical reaction with these proteins that contributes to a pink color. Smoked turkey often stays pink from the reaction of the meat to the smoke inside the grill or smoker, but even oven-roasted turkey can have a pinkish hue. Myoglobin usually turns white during the cooking process, but cytochrome c is more resistant to heat and can maintain a pink blush.

Using a meat thermometer is the best way to know if your turkey is safe to eat.

Poultry is considered safe to eat when it meets a cooking temperature of at least 165°. However, the Taste of Home Test Kitchen recommends cooking the leg and thigh meat to 170° for the best texture. For stuffed turkeys, don’t forget to take the temperature of the stuffing as well, which should reach at least 165° when the thermometer is inserted in the center of the stuffing.

If your turkey comes embedded with a round plastic doneness indicator that pops when the turkey is ready, don’t use that as an absolute; they are notoriously inaccurate.

To check if the turkey is done, insert the thermometer in a thick, meaty area, making sure the tip doesn’t touch any bones (bone will show a higher temperature).

If you’re using a probe thermometer that you insert before cooking, double-check its position once the turkey has been cooking for a while. Meat contracts as it cooks, so it may no longer be in the best spot.

If any part of your turkey is below 165°, you should continue cooking the turkey until all parts reach a safe temperature. It’s common for the thermometer to register different temperatures in different areas, since white meat cooks at a faster rate than dark meat. Don’t be tempted to cut off the parts that aren’t ready and return only them to the oven. It’ll increase the risk that undercooked juices will run onto your cutting board and contaminate the properly cooked turkey.

If the legs and thighs aren’t done but the breast is, I like to baste the white meat and loosely tent it with foil to try and lock in as much moisture as possible. If the dark meat is ready but the breast needs more time, there’s no need to sweat it. Dark meat has enough natural fat and moisture that it won’t become dry with a little extra time in the oven.

You should never knowingly eat undercooked turkey. According to the CDC, undercooked turkey can contain harmful bacteria, like Salmonella, Clostridium perfringens or Campylobacter, that can cause foodborne illnesses.

There’s also a risk of bacteria if the turkey isn’t thawed or prepared correctly. Give yourself plenty of time to thaw a frozen turkey, either in the refrigerator or in a cold water bath. Also, make sure to keep the counter or cutting board where you’re prepping the turkey clean and sanitized before and after handling the raw bird.

#6630. How to Make Whipped Cream Perfectly, Every Time

If you love a low-effort, high-reward kitchen assignment, learning how to make whipped cream is a walk in the clouds. The only ingredients are time and heavy cream. You can use an electric mixer, a whisk, or a mason jar and strong-armed devotion.

In whipped cream, and in life, the key challenge is knowing when to stop. Desserts like Strawberry Eton Mess or Triple Chocolate Mousse Cake fare best with silky, unsweetened, soft-peaked whip. Others, like this show-stopping Berries and Cream Mille-Feuille, gain structure from sturdier peaks.

To make whipped cream at home, all you need is cold heavy cream, a large bowl, and a whisk. You can also use a handheld mixer or a mason jar and some elbow grease (more on that later).

If you’re opting for a bowl-and-whisk combo, choose your tools wisely. Cream roughly doubles in volume as you whip it, so use a bowl with three to four times the capacity of your liquid. A large balloon whisk, rather than a narrow sauce whisk, helps incorporate plenty of air into the cream.

Be strategic in the dairy aisle too. Heavy cream and heavy whipping cream contain at least 36% milk fat and can be used interchangeably. Skip anything labeled simply “whipping cream”—or, heaven forbid, “light cream”—which contains less fat and won’t hold its loft as well.

For a basic batch, start with 1 cup cold heavy cream, which makes about 2 cups whipped cream. For lightly sweetened whipped cream, add 1 Tbsp. powdered sugar; for vanilla whipped cream, add ½ tsp. vanilla extract or paste.

With your equipment and ingredients in hand, there are only five steps and infinite possibilities.

Because whipped cream is usually eaten with or as dessert, you might not need to sweeten it at all. To keep flavors balanced, we tend to serve whipped cream au naturel with Bourbon Caramel Apple Pie or Diner-Style Rice Pudding.

But there are no hard-and-fast rules. Maybe you love sweetened whipped cream, or you’re serving it with something less sugary—like, say, a bowl of tart blackberries and torn mint leaves.

For lightly sweetened whipped cream, start with about 1 Tbsp. sugar per cup of cream. Powdered sugar dissolves easily and contains a little stabilizer (usually cornstarch), which can lend the whipped cream some extra holding power. Some cooks prefer the cleaner flavor of granulated sugar, which takes a little longer to dissolve. Either way, add the sugar before you start whipping.

If you’re gazing at a bowl of fluffy, ethereal whip and thinking, “Could I make this even more enchanting?” the answer is yes. There are two primary ways to make flavored whipped cream: infuse or stir.

Kitchen professionals and advance planners tend to cold-infuse. Combine your cream with flavorings like rice (for a creamy Horchata) or bourbon (to take a classic pumpkin pie over the top), then store it in the fridge anywhere from three hours to overnight. Strain out any solids before whipping.

You can also add simple flavorings, like vanilla extract, a small splash of liqueur, cocoa, ground spices, citrus zest, or coffee syrup, before you start whipping. For heavier or chunky additions, such as toasted nuts or chopped chocolate, use a rubber spatula to gently fold them in once the cream is whipped.

Peaks are the shape your whipped cream takes when you pull the whisk out of the bowl and hold it upright like the Statue of Liberty’s torch.

Soft peaks are cloudlike and slump over when you lift the whisk. Stiff peaks stand upright and hold their shape. Somewhere in between are medium peaks, which have enough structure to hold a shape while remaining soft and supple.

Most Bon Appétit recipes, such as these Mix-and-Match Fools, involve whipping cream to soft peaks. That velvety texture is our go-to when we’re dolloping whipped cream atop pecan pie.

But we aren’t always such softies. Medium peaks help this Ginger-Raspberry Icebox Cake keep its shape. And old-fashioned chocolate mousse involves whipping batches of cream into stiff and soft peaks: The former is folded into the chocolate mixture for structure, while the softer stuff tops the dessert.

By hand: Our preferred method, whipping cream by hand requires the most time and effort, but it also gives you optimal control over its final texture. Even if you use a mixer to get your whipped cream started, switching to a whisk for the final few moments makes it easier to stop exactly where you want.

In a Mason jar: No whisk? No mixer? No problem. To make whipped cream with your bare hands, put a container with a tight-fitting lid, large mason jar, or leak-proof cocktail shaker into the freezer for five minutes. Get the heavy cream very cold and make sure you have ample headspace in your vessel of choice. About one cup of liquid in a four-cup container is a good amount.

Secure the lid and shake it like you mean it. For the creamiest results, a consistently assertive pace is better than intermittent spurts of brute force. When the liquid stops sloshing and starts feeling and sounding heavier, open the lid and take a peek. If it looks underwhipped, close it back up and keep shaking.

Good news for meal preppers: You can make whipped cream hours in advance. Err on the side of underwhipping it during your prep. Store the lightly whipped cream, covered, in the fridge for up to four hours before serving, then give it a few energetic whisks to bring back its bounce right before you dollop it onto dessert.

You can also freeze whipped cream (no, seriously). It takes a bit of effort, though. Line a baking sheet with parchment, then pipe or scoop spoonfuls of whipped cream onto it. Freeze until the whipped cream nuggets are solid, then peel them off the parchment and store them in an airtight bag in the freezer for one to two months. When you’re ready to serve, let them thaw at room temperature for about 15 minutes.

Instant vanilla pudding is the key to luscious, long-lasting whipped cream.

Need it to hold up longer? Instant vanilla pudding mix is one of BA’s favorite shortcuts for stabilized whipped cream. For every cup of heavy cream, add 1 Tbsp. instant vanilla pudding mix (call it pastry cream powder if anyone gives you sass) and 2 tsp. powdered sugar, then whip as usual. The modified starch in the pudding mix absorbs excess moisture and helps prevent the cream from separating, keeping it fluffy for up to 24 hours.

For something tangier, sour cream adds both flavor and body. Our Pecan Cream Pie whisks ¼ cup sour cream into 1 cup heavy cream; the sour cream cuts the richness while helping the topping hold its shape.

In any case, your dinner party guests don’t have to sit quietly as you furiously whisk their dessert topping to order. Prep work never tasted so sweet.

If your whip isn’t coming together quite right, don’t fret. Simple solutions abound.

This is probably a temperature issue. Cold cream whips more readily and holds onto the air you’re incorporating more effectively, so it comes together faster—and stays fluffy longer. Pop the bowl, whisk, and cream back into the freezer for five minutes, or into the fridge for up to 30. Once everything is cold, resume whisking.

Another possible culprit is the fat content of your cream. Opt for heavy whipping cream or heavy cream over half-and-half or other heavy cream substitutes.

If the cream is just a little too stiff or starting to look grainy, add a splash of chilled heavy cream and slowly whisk it in. Add more, a little at a time, until the texture smooths out.

Keep a close eye on it: If you whisk for too long, you’ll end up with a bowl of butter.

Editor’s note: This story was originally published in 2017 by Julia Black. It has been substantially updated with new reporting and additional advice from the Bon Appétit archives, including contributions by Amiel Stanek, Christina Chaey, Rochelle Bilow, and Elyssa Goldberg.

#6628. Maple Pumpkin Overnight Oats

“I don’t have time” should never be an excuse to skip breakfast. Take this overnight oat–chia pudding hybrid, which comes together in barely 10 minutes. (I’m betting that’s less time than it takes to stand in line at the grocery store to buy a container of worse-tasting, more expensive oatmeal!) Grab a can of pumpkin and some baking staples, mix it up, then pop the bowl in the fridge. The next morning you’ll be rewarded with a lightly sweet, mousse-like treat that’s actually good for you—don’t forget to finish each bowl with a dollop of yogurt for a pumpkin-pie-with-whipped-cream vibe. Self-care rarely tastes this good.

Using an unsweetened soy or nut milk will keep the pudding more pumpkin-forward than dairy milk (and keeps the recipe vegan, of course), but any milk you have on hand will work here.

Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares nourishing, craveable recipes that you can pull off in 10 ingredients or fewer.

Whisk one 15-oz. can pure pumpkin purée, 1½ cups unsweetened milk of choice, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, ¼ tsp. Diamond Crystal or Morton kosher salt, ¼ cup pure maple syrup, and ½ tsp. ground cinnamon or cardamom in a large bowl until smooth. Add 3 Tbsp. chia seeds and whisk to combine. Let sit 10 minutes. (Doing this gives the seeds a head start on hydrating and prevents them from sticking together. But if you can’t spare the time, just give the mixture a good stir before serving.)

Stir chia mixture again, then add 1¼ cups old-fashioned oats and mix well to combine. Cover oat mixture and chill at least 8 hours.

Spoon oat mixture into bowls and top with plain whole-milk yogurt, unsalted roasted pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or granola, maple syrup, and cinnamon as desired.

Do Ahead: Oat mixture (without toppings) can be made 4 days ahead. Keep chilled.

#6627. Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

Personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

The same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

Sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

Green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

Turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The great and "godless" English philosopher Jeremy Bentham, whose remains have been on display at a U.K. university for over 150 years, suffered from severe dental problems, according to X-ray scans of his skull.

The scans were conducted with CT (computed tomography) scanning equipment to create a digital 3D model of his head and highlight Bentham's lengthy "presence" at University College London (UCL) as it celebrates its 200th anniversary.

The scans revealed that Bentham was missing many teeth and had advanced arthritis in his lower jaw when he died of natural causes at the age of 84. During the scanning process, project leader Tannis Davidson, curator of UCL's Grant Museum of Zoology, saw how thin the jawbone had become. "He must have been in excruciating pain," she told Live Science.

Bentham's utilitarian philosophy inspired UCL's founders; it was only the third university in England, after Oxford and Cambridge, which was founded as London University in 1826 and opened to students in 1828.

As a young man, Bentham had declared that he would donate his body to science after his death. This was a radical idea at the time; in the U.K., dissection after death was looked down upon, even if it was for scientific purposes, and it was reserved for the worst criminals. After Bentham died in 1832, his remains were fashioned into an auto-icon — a supposed replica of himself — to memorialize him in the way a tombstone might, Davidson said.

Except for brief visits across Europe and to the Met Breuer in New York City, this auto-icon has been in a display case at UCL since the 1850s, where it can be seen by students as they pass by.

To make the auto-icon (which is not a mummy), Bentham's body was dissected and studied. Then, his skeleton was dressed in his clothes, which were padded with straw. His severed head was badly disfigured during an attempt to preserve it with sulfuric acid, so a wax reconstruction based on paintings and death masks was attached to the body.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Bentham's real head was displayed at the feet of the clothed skeleton that had a lifelike wax head; the real head's eyes were replaced with highly detailed glass eyes, which can be seen in the scans. According to UCL lore, the real head was stolen in 1975 and held ransom for a few days by rivals from King's College London, after which it was locked away.

Davidson explained that Bentham had coined the term "auto-icon" to mean "self-representation" and was setting an example for others. "He imagined a future where people were making auto-icons to keep their dead relatives around," she said.

The CT scans of the real head show that Bentham had dental damage and jaw arthritis, and that his brain had been removed before it was preserved—although some of his dura mater, a layer of connective tissue that covers the brain and spinal cord, was preserved. Davidson said the brain extraction was done to keep with Bentham's instructions that his head be mummified in the same way as Māori heads, which had their brains removed. The scanning process is shown in a short film called "Bentham Revealed."

Jeremy Bentham's "auto-icon" on display at University College London in 2008.

Bentham wrote about his dental problems several times, Davidson said, but it is not clear if he understood that he also had severe arthritis in his lower jaw, which must have made the problems with his teeth much more painful. In addition, modern ideas about cleaning teeth had not been established by Bentham's time. "Dentistry 200 years ago was a very different kettle of fish than it is today," Davidson said.

Bentham was a polymath who hoped to improve the lives of ordinary people through social reform. He wrote extensively about subjects as varied as law, economics, education and animal rights, and he believed that society could be engineered to produce better outcomes through legislation and the objective measurement of "utility."

His most famous idea was the panopticon in 1791, a ring-shaped prison with one warden to watch all of the prisoners, which he proposed as a humane alternative to Australia's penal colonies. Today, however, it is a symbol of state control and surveillance. Bentham also invented a "felicific calculus" to numerically assess the benefits and drawbacks of any given action, based on variables like its intensity, duration, certainty, purity and extent.

Bentham's philosophy put him at odds with the established Church of England; he called himself an "unbeliever," while critics called him "godless."

This rift with the church may have played a part in Bentham's wishes for his remains. Davidson suggested that the auto-icon may have been a means for Bentham to avoid being buried with traditional Anglican rites. "Maybe this was a way he could 'stick it to them' a little bit," she said.

Tom Metcalfe is a freelance journalist and regular Live Science contributor who is based in London in the United Kingdom. Tom writes mainly about science, space, archaeology, the Earth and the oceans. He has also written for the BBC, NBC News, National Geographic, Scientific American, Air & Space, and many others.

The right baking pan can be the difference between a cake that releases cleanly and one that falls apart. Here's why hybrid bakeware is catching our attention.

So what exactly is hybrid bakeware, and is it worth the kitchen upgrade? Let’s take a closer look.

Traditional bakeware usually features one primary material, such as aluminum, stainless steel or glass. Hybrid bakeware, on the other hand, takes a different approach by pairing multiple materials together. For example, durable stainless steel pairs with an easy-release ceramic nonstick coating. You get the best of both worlds in one pan.

Stainless steel and ceramic nonstick make a pretty dynamic duo in baking. Stainless steel delivers durability and provides a sturdy baking surface, while nonstick helps prevent baked goods from sticking to the pan.

Hybrid bakeware can make everyday baking easier, from achieving consistent oven results to releasing delicate treats without damage. “Those everyday details matter to me when I’m deciding what deserves space in my kitchen,” explains D’Aniello.

#6624. 11 Leftover Turkey Sandwiches to Look Forward To

It is a universal truth that the food the day after Thanksgiving is just as exciting (if not more so) as what’s served on the holiday itself. With a fridge full of Thanksgiving leftovers, the possibilities are endless. But leftovers reach their most perfect form in a sandwich, where all the components play off one other for a few transcendent bites.

These Thanksgiving sandwiches make the most of what you’ve got, whether that’s a few slices of turkey or enough stuffing and cranberry sauce for an encore. Go all in with a gooey melt, load a pita with spiced turkey and crunchy vegetables, or give turkey the chicken salad treatment. There’s no need for post-holiday blues when a leftover turkey sandwich is on the horizon.

This turkey sandwich takes inspiration from one of the all-time greats: the tuna melt. You might be surprised by how well turkey takes to the format. For the full diner experience, serve it with potato chips and a dill pickle.

These leftover turkey sliders have a lot going on, in the best way. Picture: melty cheese, cranberry mayo, garlic butter, turkey, mashed potatoes, and more where that came from.

Give your Thanksgiving leftovers the club treatment by layering turkey and cranberry sauce with crisp bacon and lettuce. And don’t forget that middle slide of bread. We’re not animals, after all.

Need a break from heavy Thanksgiving fare but still have turkey to use up? Shred it, toss it with butter-bloomed spices, and tuck it into a pita with a bright, tangy slaw.

In this play on a turkey club, the middle slice of bread gets swapped out for leftover stuffing fried in bacon fat. (We repeat: stuffing fried in bacon fat.)

Turkey and cranberry sauce already have a salty-sweet thing going on. Why not play that up by swapping plain bread for custardy French toast?

Sometimes it’s best to keep a leftover turkey sandwich simple. Turkey, cranberry sauce, cheese, and fresh sage, pressed until golden, give you all the flavors of Thanksgiving in four ingredients (plus bread).

Though the recipe calls for cooked chicken, you guessed it—you can swap in leftover turkey seamlessly. The apple and fennel both provide lots of crunch and freshness.

Another chicken banger that works beautifully with leftover turkey. Boosted with red curry paste, tangy from Greek yogurt, this mixture is as good stuffed into lettuce cups as it is tucked between sliced bread.

This recipe sticks close to the classic turkey club, with one simple twist: a punchy, verdant herb mayo that comes together in seconds in the blender.

Roast turkey, tangy sauerkraut, melty Swiss cheese, and a tangy sauce? Heaven. Bonus points if the rye bread you use is studded with caraway seeds.

#6623. 25 Midwestern Thanksgiving Recipes That Bring The Nostalgia (& The Flavor)

Even nicer than Midwest nice (and that's saying something!).

My holidays were split between regions growing up. We spent Thanksgiving at my dad’s side, and Christmas with my mom’s. With my mom’s Alabama and Texas roots and my dad's Missouri and Kansas roots, that meant that Christmas dinner was a Southern affair and Thanksgiving was a Midwestern feast. Both holiday spreads had a fair amount of overlap of dishes (casseroles galore), but I have to say: A classic Midwest Thanksgiving has a special place in my heart.

What makes a Midwest Thanksgiving, you may ask? All of the classics are present, plus a few surprising favorites that, in my house, no holiday is complete without. We think beyond the turkey, sometimes skip mashed potatoes for a cheesy casserole, and have to be careful not to fill up on all the rolls (butter and honey better be on the table). Ready to celebrate Midwest-style? Here are some recipes that your holiday won’t be complete without:

Made with canned pineapple, pistachio pudding, and Cool Whip, this retro crowd-pleasing dessert “salad” will take you straight back to the ’70s with just one bite. It’s the perfect recipe to throw together if you don’t have a ton of time, but you need to take something to that potluck or family gathering.

Thanksgiving is equally about food and football, so this tailgate-inspired stuffing is a no-brainer. Filled with beer cheese sauce and topped with crispy bacon, this twist on the classic holiday side is so irresistible, it’ll be gone long before halftime of that first Thanksgiving Day game.

It takes less than than 5 minutes to pour some pepper jelly over cream cheese and place some crackers around. These bites are slightly more elevated without many more steps. It’s for those that want to feel like they are putting some effort into their appetizer without it being difficult or time-consuming.

Don't be fooled by the name—the only thing deathly about this casserole is how absolutely delicious it is. This cheesy, creamy casserole is a staple at every holiday in my Kansas home, and Thanksgiving is no exception. Yes, we often have mashed potatoes too.

For this recipe, we ditched canned cream of mushroom soup and went for fresh instead. It's not how my mom makes it, but trust me—by sautéing mushrooms with sliced onion in butter, you're building a base with some serious depth of flavor. Cook the mushrooms enough that they get a little caramelized, and you'll really be good to go.

No matter the holiday, one thing is for sure: Deviled eggs will be making an appearance. Variations are always welcome (looking at you, harissa deviled eggs), but if grandpa is going to have a happy Thanksgiving, then this classic recipe better be present.

Strawberry pretzel tart, AKA strawberry pretzel salad, might sound a little strange, but trust us—it strikes the perfect balance of whimsical and classic, sweet and salty. The pretzel crust proves to be an ideal complement to the rich cream cheese layer and the sweet strawberries with their Jell-O glaze.

Turkey usually rules the roost at Thanksgiving, but it's not the only centerpiece present at many Midwestern holiday tables. Depending on how many family members are coming, my family has been known to prepare a turkey and a ham—it's the best of both worlds!

We’re certainly not opposed to roasted Brussels sprouts, but we also love giving them the traditional Thanksgiving treatment—plenty of butter, cream, and cheese. This method upgrades even the most humble vegetables while still allowing them to be the star of the show.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for. Plus, you can easily make it ahead and travel with it, making it an ideal potluck recipe.

These Thanksgiving potato skins are piled high with leftovers, but they’re so good, they just might deserve a place in your holiday spread. The hollowed-out potatoes are an excellent vessel for extra-creamy mashed potatoes, stuffing, turkey, and dollops of cranberry sauce.

Essentially, this is chicken Alfredo, but with a few extra decadent add-ins, like cream cheese, garlic, and punchy spices like nutmeg and black pepper. When you’re craving the classic but have to serve a crowd, this is the recipe you should make.

A cheese ball is peak party appetizer nostalgia, and these cheese ball bites are here to put a new, shareable twist on the classic. They’re so simple to make, only require a handful of ingredients, and are super versatile based on what you have on hand.

I'll clarify that when I say stuffing, I'm actually referring to dressing. Traditional stuffing should be stuffed inside the turkey and cooked in there, but in my family, we've always called it stuffing. By cooking your stuffing in a baking dish, you get crunchy, buttery pieces of bread on top and soft, bread pudding-esque pieces underneath.

What’s the best kind of potato? A loaded baked potato, of course. With this in mind, we combined the two superstar spuds into one glorious dish. In it, light, airy mashed potatoes are topped with all of the classic baked potato fillings—cheddar cheese, chives, bacon, and sour cream—for a dish that truly embodies the best of both worlds.

Most sweet potato casseroles have only marshmallows or pecans. Don't even think about making this mistake. Topping with a pecan streusel and then marshmallows helps this Thanksgiving casserole stand out above all the rest.

If you’re not into creamy, melty macaroni and cheese with a wildly satisfying cheese-pull, then you might want to find another mac recipe. Sorry, but this slow-cooker macaroni and cheese is just too darn dreamy.

Step aside, all other casseroles—corn is not to be overlooked on the holiday table. If you prefer, drained and rinsed canned corn can be used instead of frozen, and you could substitute more milk in for the heavy cream. The finished casserole won't be quite as decadent, but it will still be delicious.

Deviled eggs are great, but when you have them for every holiday, it just makes sense to change them up sometimes. These are our new obsession

If green beans dressed up as cheesy garlic bread, then they would become these Parmesan roasted green beans. Tossed in garlic and black pepper and showered with cheese, this simply irresistible side dish will steal the spotlight at every holiday table.

This sweet party dip is the perfect way to add that little extra something to your fruit spread, but your dipping options don't stop there! With just 5 minutes of prep, this is the easiest dessert that any party will be thankful for.

A genetic analysis has identified two previously unrecognized species of howler monkey that change these primates' evolutionary tree.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Scientists have identified two newfound species of howler monkey in the Amazon rainforest. The discoveries could redraw branches of these primates' evolutionary tree, a new study shows.

The new species were named Alouatta iroi and Alouatta matogrossensis. The adorable creatures have bushy beards, winsome expressions and bright red fur. Their identification raises the number of known howler monkey species to 16, researchers said in a statement.

"Our study shows that the Amazon still holds remarkable biological secrets, even among well-known animals such as howler monkeys," study first author Romina Batista, a biodiversity scientist at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

One of the newfound species, A. matogrossensis, is probably on the brink of extinction. The other newfound species faces threats from a planned dam on the Rio Branco River, according to the study.

In addition to identifying the new species, the study, published Oct. 30 in the journal Communications Biology, used genetic evidence to understand when howler monkeys spread out and diversified. The researchers analyzed the genomes of 11 howler monkey species living in South and Central America, combining existing DNA datasets with new genomic information from specimens in Brazilian zoological collections.

The newfound howler monkey species Alouatta iroi, photographed in Guiana.

Overall, the genetic data confirmed that howler monkeys diverged from close relatives between 19 million and 13.5 million years ago. But the analysis changed the picture of more recent evolution.

For instance, the team argued that the Tapajós red-handed howler (A. tapajozensis) and the Amazonian black howler (A. nigerrima) are not as closely related as scientists previously thought. The researchers also said that the Trinidad howler (A. insulanus), whose status has been unclear, should be confirmed as a separate species.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"This discovery comes at a critical time, as increasing deforestation, climate change and habitat loss threaten many Amazonian species before they are fully understood or even discovered by science," study co-author Jean Boubli, a professor and chair of primate ecology and evolution at the University of Salford in the U.K., said in the statement.

The scientists found that natural barriers such as the Amazon River, the Xingu River and the Branco River drove many howler monkeys to develop separately. Researchers believe that howler monkeys can swim across small waterways, but big rivers block groups from mixing, which led to different traits and species evolving over time. Natural barriers are a common reason why species emerge in the Amazon, the researchers noted in the study.

#6621. 10 Holiday Groceries Our Editors Are Stocking Up on This Year

From the perfect cracker for a cheese board to the best puff pastry for holiday baking, these are the grocery store finds our editors can't get enough of this holiday season.

Our editors and experts handpick every product we feature. We may earn a commission from your purchases.Learn more.

October through December is a magical time at the supermarket, when the aisles transform into a treasure trove of new foods for the holidays. It’s all of our favorite snacks, but in the coziest seasonal flavors.

We’re on a mission to discover the hottest new groceries all year long, so when seasonal and limited-time items hit the shelves, you know we’re stocking up on the best of the best.

From stuffing-inspired potato chips to fizzy cranberry drinks, these are the holiday items worth seeking out the next time you’re at the grocery store.

“A hill I will die on? Cranberry is the best fall flavor. This soda has the fresh, fizzy bubbles I’ve come to expect from lemon-lime Poppi—but with a subtle twist. The cranberry flavor hits you on the back end of your palate and adds a subtle twang to a standard white soda. Cranberry Fizz Poppi is ideal for sipping on its own or pairing with cranberry juice for a more prominent flavor.” —Katie Bandurski, deputy shopping editor

“Disclaimer: Peppermint is not normally my holiday flavor of choice. I’m much more into the eggnog and gingerbread of it all. But when Sprouts came out with a new peppermint chocolate version of its famous Gluten-Free coconut rolls, I had to look past my ‘won’t this just taste like eating a candy cane?’ aversion. It turns out that Sprouts found just the right balance of mint, bitter dark chocolate and just-sweet enough coconut milk—three flavors that I still can’t believe work this well together.

Texturally, these coconut rolls are outstanding. The light, crispy rolls, coated in snappy chocolate and crunchy snowflake sprinkles, are so easy to eat that I finished the entire bag in two days.” —Val Goodrich, food writer

“I grabbed these stuffing-flavored kettle chips at the Trader Joe’s checkout line last week, and I need to go back to buy about 10 more bags. There’s something about the salty, crunchy kettle chips paired with the spot-on flavorings of herby stuffing that make these THE fall snack. The notes of sage and thyme come through in every bite without being overpowering.” —KB

“I like to prep homemade pistachio milk and pistachio syrup for my iced lattes in the morning on a semi-regular basis, but somehow I never thought to use pistachio milk to make a peppermint mocha. Tache’s new peppermint mocha pistachio milk means that I can have a pepperminty, decadent and rich iced pistachio peppermint mocha with just a carton and espresso—no time-consuming homemade syrups or sauces necessary.

This milk is made for putting in coffee, but I’ll even drink it plain, without any added espresso, because it’s just that good. Tache also recommends shaking it with espresso and vodka to make an espresso martini, which sounds like a perfect holiday cocktail. —Lauren Pahmeier, editor

“Casting my love of the Great British Baking Show aside, where someone is always rolling out rough puff and traditional puff, everyone knows buying puff pastry versus making it from scratch is a clutch move. Especially during the holidays when there are so many other things to make.

Trader Joe’s all-butter puff pastry version is only available during the fall and winter months and it flies off the shelves, so I always stock up and buy several boxes at a time. It’s the best all-butter frozen puff pastry for the price (two rectangle sheets for less than $6!), and it doesn’t have any fillers or preservatives. It tastes great, puffs nicely and can be used for on-the-fly appetizers and pretty desserts when company drops in.” —Lesley Balla, editor

“Pretzels and apple pie aren’t really something I would have pictured as a pair. But when I discovered this unique combination at a food show last year, I knew I had to take a bag of Pop Daddy’s Dutch Apple Pie Seasoned Pretzels home with me. The apple flavor combined with the cinnamon-sugar coating makes me think of messy apple cider doughnuts. The apple pie pretzels are my top choice but I love Pop Daddy’s gluten-free tomato basil pretzels and smoked Gouda pretzels, too.” —LP

“I love a good pistachio ice cream, and this pistachio macaron-inspired option from Jeni’s has it all. It’s sweet, salty and nutty, with an unforgettable texture that captures the chewiness of a macaron. The slight almond flavor complements the other ingredients without being overpowering. I also like the natural hue of this ice cream rather than the bright green often associated with pistachio ice cream.” —KB

“I don’t say this lightly, but Haymaker Bun Company’s sticky buns might actually rival my mom’s Christmas morning cinnamon rolls. (Sorry, Mom.) I made them for my family on a rainy Saturday morning and they were spectacular. The buttery brioche is impossibly soft, with generous swirls of cinnamon and all the sticky, gooey goodness you want from a cinnamon roll. They’re made in Vermont, shipped frozen and ready after just 15 minutes in the oven, which seems like an almost unreasonable amount of convenience for something so delicious. I’m already trying to justify keeping a permanent supply in my freezer.” —Lindsay Parill, trends writer

“They say the cheese is supposed to be the star of a cheese board, but these Trader Joe’s crackers give any wedge some serious competition. They’re thin with a crisp like a crouton and speckled with dried mission figs, briny kalamata olives, and a mix of seeds for a balance of sweet, savory and hearty.

Aperitivo (aka snacking before dinner) is sacred in my house, and my go-to is a circle of these crisps surrounding a bowl of whipped ricotta with sea salt and a drizzle of good balsamic. On a full cheese or charcuterie board, I’ll pair them with pretty much any soft or spreadable cheese, plus fig jam, honey and halved grapes. Buy an extra box—they’ll disappear quickly!” —Rachel Vigoda, senior deputy editor

#6620. Pineapple Chaat

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

#6619. Popeyes Beat KFC In My Chicken Sandwich Showdown—But Can It Take Down Chick-fil-A?

The chicken sandwich wars are far from over.

Few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

Chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

My biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be said for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

Popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

The mayo was another important part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

While Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

Chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.
